faq.a: No; many are innocent and require no treatment, but any new or changing murmur in an adult warrants evaluation.
Severe anaemia from malaria can produce a flow murmur, which resolves when the anaemia is corrected.
Valsalva or standing reduces preload, intensifying the systolic ejection murmur of HCM.
faq.q: What bedside manoeuvre helps differentiate hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?

exam: A 22‑year‑old with a grade III systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla – what is the most likely diagnosis and next investigation? — Mitral regurgitation; obtain echocardiography to assess severity.
A child from a rural clinic has a soft, blowing systolic murmur that disappears with sitting forward – how would you classify it? — Innocent flow murmur; no further cardiac work‑up needed.

A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive patient presents with fever, a new holosystolic murmur, and splinter haemorrhages – what is the priority management step? — Obtain three sets of blood cultures and start empiric IV antibiotics for possible infective endocarditis.

In a patient with known rheumatic mitral stenosis, what sign on auscultation indicates progression to severe disease? — Loud opening snap followed by a low‑pitch rumble and a prominent atrial contraction sound.
How does squatting affect a murmur of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and why? — Increases preload, reducing the murmur intensity; demonstrates dynamic outflow obstruction.

A pregnant woman in her second trimester develops a grade II diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge – what is the likely cause? — Physiological increased flow across the aortic valve; reassurance and observation.

When echocardiography is unavailable, what clinical criteria help decide referral for surgical valve repair? — Symptoms of heart failure, murmur grade ≥III, evidence of chamber enlargement on chest X‑ray, and atrial fibrillation.
Why should NSAIDs be avoided in a patient with rheumatic heart disease and concurrent malaria? — NSAIDs can worsen renal impairment and mask fever, complicating malaria management.
ai.title: Cardiac Murmur
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: A cardiac murmur is a sound produced by turbulent blood flow in the heart or great vessels. Recognising patterns helps differentiate innocent from pathological murmurs and guides further investigation and management, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Innocent murmurs are common in children and young adults and usually benign.
Pathological murmurs may indicate valve disease, septal defects, or high‑output states.
sections.p: Murmurs are graded I–VI and described by timing (systolic, diastolic, continuous), location, radiation, shape and manoeuvre response. In low‑resource hospitals, many are first identified by bedside auscultation.

b: Systolic ejection murmurs: crescendo‑decrescendo, best at the aortic or pulmonic areas.
Holosystolic murmurs: plateau‑shaped, radiate to the axilla (mitral) or to the back (tricuspid).
Diastolic murmurs: decrescendo (aortic regurg) or rumbling (mitral stenosis).
sections.p: Distinguish murmur types, apply the modified WHO criteria for rheumatic heart disease, and use simple bedside manoeuvres (e.g., squatting, Valsalva) to clarify the diagnosis.

b: Rheumatic mitral regurgitation is the leading cause of heart failure in young adults.
Severe aortic stenosis may present with syncope, angina, and heart failure.
Uncorrected ventricular septal defect can cause pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger syndrome.
sections.p: In East African hospitals, common causes of pathological murmurs include rheumatic heart disease, congenital septal defects, endocarditis (often HIV‑related), and anemia from malaria or sickle‑cell disease.

t.b: What is the murmur’s timing, intensity and radiation? – Confirms type and suggests valve involvement.
Is there chamber enlargement or conduction abnormality? – Supports valve disease or shunt physiology.
Is there cardiomegaly or pulmonary congestion? – Helps stage severity.
What is valve anatomy, gradient and regurgitant volume? – Gold standard for diagnosis and severity.
Is anemia present? – Explains high‑output murmurs and guides treatment.

b: Rheumatic valve disease: secondary prophylaxis with benzathine penicillin G every 4 weeks; avoid NSAIDs that may worsen renal function in malaria‑co‑infection.
Severe aortic stenosis: refer for valve replacement; give diuretics only for pulmonary congestion.
Ventricular septal defect with heart failure: start diuretics and ACE‑inhibitors; plan surgical closure when feasible.
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, provide symptomatic relief, and arrange definitive referral when surgery is needed.

b: A pericardial friction rub is triphasic and louder on inspiration.
Carotid bruit is heard over the neck and disappears with neck compression.
sections.p: Distinguish murmurs from extra‑cardiac sounds such as pericardial rubs, carotid bruits, or respiratory wheezes.

b: A quiet murmur in a patient with severe heart failure does not exclude severe valve disease.
Normal ECG does not rule out structural valve lesions.
sections.p: In severe anemia, flow murmurs may mimic valvular disease; conversely, low‑output states can mask a murmur.

b: When a new murmur appears in a febrile patient, think infective endocarditis and order blood cultures.
sections.p: Exam questions often test pattern recognition, appropriate next step, and management priorities.

whenToSeekHelp: New or changing murmur with chest pain, syncope, or heart failure signs
Severe dyspnoea or orthopnoea indicating acute decompensation
